name: Why Is It Called the Shelf?
author: Shelf oral tradition — compiled by a community archivist in Block 7
description:
New arrivals always ask. Kids born here don't, because they understand it the way you understand gravity — it's just the shape of the world. But if you need it explained: look up.

Everything sits on top of us. The Circuit. The Laceworks. The Core. The Spires. Two hundred years of construction, each generation building on top of the last, and every time they built up they pushed us down. We are the foundation. We are the shelf that the city sits on. The load-bearing floor. The surface everything else was placed upon and then forgotten about, the way you forget about a shelf once you've put something on it. You don't look at the shelf. You look at what's on the shelf. We're not on the shelf. We are the shelf.

It wasn't always this way. Old-timers — the ones who remember the early construction booms of the 2100s — say there was a time when ground level was just ground level. Streets. Sky. Sun. Then the first overpasses went up, and the elevated transit, and the skyways between buildings, and the platforms, and the second-story commercial strips, and the third-story residential bands, and by the time anyone thought to ask what was happening to the people who lived at street level, street level was four stories below the new ground. The sun came through in slices. Then slivers. Then not at all.

The name came from the residents, not the planners. The planners called it Sub-Grade Residential Zone 1. The residents called it the Shelf, because that's what it felt like — being put on a shelf and left there. A thing stored. A thing not thrown away but not used either. The name stuck because it was true twice: we are the shelf the city sits on, and we are on the shelf — set aside, out of the way, bearing the weight of everything above us without being seen by any of it.

There's a third meaning the old-timers use. Shelf life. As in: how long before something stored on a shelf expires. How long before the foundation gives way. How long before the weight becomes too much. Nobody says this one out loud. But when the pipes groan at night and the ceiling — which is someone else's floor — creaks with the mass of fourteen stories of other people's lives, you think it. Everyone in the Shelf thinks it. How long before the shelf breaks.
story_hooks: A structural engineer publishes a report — quickly suppressed — calculating that three specific Shelf districts are bearing loads they were never designed for. The foundations are original 21st-century concrete. They were built to support six stories. They are currently supporting forty. The engineer's models predict failure within fifteen years. The report is titled: "Shelf Life."
